 Kenya fuel prices: Will EPRA reduce petrol, diesel and kerosene prices on November 14?
 Sunday 08th November, 2026 02:45 PM | 
 By Aloys Michael 
 Fuel pumps at a petrol station. PHOTO/@EPRA_KE/X 
 Kenyans are hoping for cheaper petrol, diesel and kerosene as i nternational oil prices fall by nearly 15 per cent ahead of the November 14 fuel price review, while Treasury Cabinet Secretary John Mbadi signals plans to use government stabilisation funds to cushion consumers.
 The developments have raised expectations that motorists could finally get relief after the October fuel price increase pushed Super Petrol to Ksh226.96 per litre, Diesel to Ksh227.76 and Kerosene to Ksh219.87 in Nairobi.
 However, whether prices will actually decline, remain unchanged, or increase depends on the cost of imported petroleum products and the government’s planned intervention.
 The Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority (EPRA) is expected to announce the new maximum retail prices on November 14, with the revised rates taking effect at midnight for the November 15 to December 14 pricing period.
 A petrol station attendant fuelling a vehicle in Nairobi. PHOTO/John Ochieng 
 Will prices fall? 
 There are two major developments supporting expectations of cheaper fuel in Kenya .
 First, international oil prices have declined significantly. Second, the government has indicated that it intends to deploy money from the Petroleum Development Levy stabilisation fund to cushion consumers during the November-December pricing cycle.
 Speaking during a November 3 interview on a local vernacular Radio station, Mbadi explained that the government deliberately avoided using the fund during the October review to preserve resources for the following month.
 “So we projected that fuel prices in November might go up, so we did not use the funds last month so that we can use them this month to reduce the prices of fuel,” Mbadi said.
 His remarks suggest that the government wants to prevent another painful increase and potentially lower the amount consumers pay at petrol stations.
 However, the CS did not disclose the amount of the proposed subsidy or specify how much each litre of fuel could become cheaper.
 Ships in Strait of Hormuz. PHOTO/@GreaterKashmir/X 
 Oil prices retreat 
 The strongest indication of possible relief comes from the international petroleum market.
 According to the Central Bank of Kenya’s November 6 Weekly Bulletin, Murban crude oil prices declined to US$94.04 per barrel on November 5, from US$110.46 on October 29.
 That represents a drop of approximately 14.86 per cent in one week.
 The CBK attributed the decline to easing financial market conditions following the US midterm elections and reduced expectations of disruptions to oil supplies from the Middle East.
 The development is significant for Kenya, which relies on imported petroleum products to meet domestic demand.
 A reduction in international petroleum costs can eventually translate into cheaper fuel imports, potentially creating room for lower pump prices.
 The Kenyan shilling also remained stable at Ksh129.96 against the US dollar on November 5, unchanged from October 29, according to the CBK.
 Currency stability matters because petroleum imports are purchased in foreign currencies. A weaker shilling could otherwise offset some of the benefits of declining international oil prices.
 Nevertheless, crude oil prices are not the same as the landed costs of refined petrol, diesel and kerosene used in EPRA’s pricing calculations.
 Central Bank of Kenya headquarters. PHOTO/@StocksMarket_ke/X 
 Why prices may resist 
 Despite the positive developments, a fuel price reduction is not guaranteed .
 In October, EPRA Director-General Edward Mwirigi Kinyua warned that international market pressures could persist into November and December, explaining why the regulator had opted to preserve stabilisation resources.
 The regulator also reported substantial increases in the landed costs of imported petroleum products between August and September.
 Kinyua described September as “the worst month ever since this crisis broke,” according to Pulse Kenya.
 This highlights the challenge facing policymakers: a temporary decline in crude oil prices does not necessarily erase earlier increases in the cost of importing refined petroleum products.
 EPRA must consider the applicable average import costs, exchange rates, taxes, levies, distribution expenses and any government stabilisation intervention before determining the new maximum retail prices.
 Consequently, motorists could receive a reduction, experience relatively unchanged prices or face another increase if import costs remain elevated.
 Matatus and other vehicles in Nairobi. PHOTO/@RoadSafetyNGOs/X 
 What motorists pay 
 Under the current EPRA pricing schedule, the maximum retail prices in Nairobi for October 15 to November 14 are: Super Petrol: Ksh226.96 per litre, Diesel: Ksh227.76 per litre, and Kerosene: Ksh219.87 per litre.
 The October review increased petrol by Ksh12.93, diesel by Ksh9.90 and kerosene by Ksh28.49 per litre.
 The increases have implications beyond motorists. Higher diesel prices can raise transportation and production expenses, potentially increasing the cost of food and other essential commodities. Kerosene increases particularly affect households relying on the fuel for cooking and lighting.
 A reduction could therefore provide relief to households, public transport operators and businesses.
 The November 14 decision will be crucial. Falling international oil prices, a stable shilling and Mbadi’s proposed intervention provide reasons for cautious optimism. However, until EPRA publishes its official figures, no specific reduction can be guaranteed.
 For millions of Kenyans, the central question remains whether these favourable developments will finally translate into cheaper fuel from November 15.
